Stories / Madrid · Andalusia · Extremadura · 1812

Story · Peninsular War, 19th century

The Tagus, 1812: eight weeks before Salamanca, Jourdan’s ciphered order to Soult

Spring 1812: Wellington has taken Ciudad Rodrigo and Badajoz; he is about to march on Salamanca. On 19 May General Hill destroys the pontoon bridge at Almaraz, the only solid crossing of the Tagus between the French armies of the north and the south. On the 28th, from Madrid, Marshal Jourdan, King Joseph’s chief of staff, writes in cipher to Marshal Soult in Andalusia. The letter is intercepted; the Spanish translate it but leave the cipher numbers as they are.

Story by Brice Dudout · reading with Claude · document: Archivo Histórico Nacional (Madrid), DIVERSOS-COLECCIONES, 134, N.34 · published 14 November 2026

« Vous sentez, monsieur le maréchal, que dans cette circonstance vous devez renforcer le corps du comte d’Erlon autant que cela vous sera possible. »

“You will feel, Monsieur le Maréchal, that in this circumstance you must reinforce the corps of the Count d’Erlon as far as you can”: Jourdan to Soult, Madrid, 28 May 1812 (ciphered passage, read with the Grand Chiffre table).

What is new, what was known

Known. The 1812 quarrel between King Joseph and Soult, who refused to strip Andalusia, is well known to historians.[3] On the same day Jourdan wrote Marmont a parallel letter, printed in Marmont’s Mémoires. The 1812 “Grand Chiffre” is famous: George Scovell broke much of it for Wellington.[4] The Madrid item is listed in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (file no. 751).[2]

What we add, to our knowledge. (1) The first published decipherment of the letter to Soult, which is missing from Scovell’s list of ciphers: read, 259 of 267 numbers (97.0%), 250 of them certain. (2) Textual proof that the orders sent to Soult repeated those given to Marmont and d’Erlon. (3) A lead on the “paper” Wellington reproached the Marquis of Monsalud for not sending him.

The spring of 1812

In Spain four French armies shared the country: Marmont (Army of Portugal) in the north, around Salamanca; Soult (Army of the South) in Andalusia; King Joseph and the Army of the Centre in Madrid. Napoleon, preparing the Russian campaign, had given the king supreme command, with Jourdan as chief of staff; Soult would not accept it.[3] By destroying Almaraz, Hill cut the shortest road between Marmont and Soult. In Madrid it was feared that Wellington would fall on one or the other.

The order of 28 May

The plain part of the letter, translated into Spanish, sums up Marmont’s news: Wellington is north of the Tagus with his whole army, except Hill’s division. Then comes the cipher, which we read in French, the language of the original:

“The Duke of Ragusa has called the Foy division back to him, so that only three battalions and about eight hundred horse of the Army of the Centre will remain in the Tagus valley […]. You will feel, Monsieur le Maréchal, that in this circumstance you must reinforce the corps of the Count d’Erlon as far as you can, so as to put it in a state to beat General Hill’s corps if it stays on the Guadiana. If on the contrary Lord Wellington calls General Hill back to him, then the Count d’Erlon must move on Miravete and come and cross the Tagus at the bridge of Arzobispo, to cover Madrid or to move on the right flank of the English army, as circumstances require.”

The plan is plain: d’Erlon (Drouet), detached from Soult’s army, must either hold Hill in Extremadura or come up to the Tagus to cover Madrid and threaten Wellington’s flank. The crossing at Arzobispo, Jourdan adds, is difficult for artillery, “but it is not impracticable”.

Eight weeks later

Soult did not follow these orders: he kept his troops in Andalusia and d’Erlon stayed facing Hill.[3] In June Wellington entered Salamanca. On 22 July, at the Arapiles, he beat Marmont, alone; the Army of the Centre, which left Madrid too late, did not arrive. On 12 August Wellington entered Madrid.[5] The letter of 28 May catches the moment when Joseph’s staff still saw the danger coming and tried to concentrate its forces.

It was copied in Extremadura and initialled “Monsalud”. On 11 June Wellington wrote to Hill that the Marquis of Monsalud believed Joseph had ordered Soult to draw nearer the Tagus, but had not sent him “the paper” on which he based that idea.[6] That paper might be this one; it is only a hypothesis. Even if passed on, it would have stayed partly unreadable: the Spanish did not have the key.

The record, text and translation →

The Grand Chiffre of 1812

  • A code of 1,200 numbers for letters, syllables and words, extended to 1,400 by additions for Spain (1211 = the Army of the Centre, 1214 = the English army, 1300 = Lord Wellington, 1383 = the Tagus).
  • Homophones: several numbers for frequent words.
  • The decoding table is kept at the Service historique de la Défense (“B n° 30”); we read it on Jean-François Bouchaudy’s photographs, which are not reproduced here.

How we read it

  1. Transcription of the 267 numbers from the PARES images, frozen by SHA-256 fingerprint before any reading of the table.
  2. Reading the cells needed in the table, list frozen before decoding; only seven cells re-read afterwards on the image, recorded separately.
  3. A held-out validation, under a protocol written beforehand: the French likelihood of the mechanical decoding (trigrams learned from an independent text, Marmont’s Mémoires) is compared with that of 1,000 tables in which the same values are dealt out at random. On this letter none equals it (−2.145 against −2.209 at the 99th percentile).
  4. The reading: 250 certain numbers, 9 probable, 8 restored from the sense (errors of the Spanish copyist, who confuses 1 and 7, 3 and 9, 5 and 6), none unresolved.

What remains uncertain

  • A copy of a copy. We read a period Spanish translation; the original French text has not been found.
  • A validation with a small margin. The gap with the controls is clear in rank (0 in 1,000) but small in value; the key’s strength lies mainly in its being the period table itself.
  • Marmont’s letter of 1 June, in the same file and the same cipher, is read only in part (≈ 85%): the Spanish copy is too faulty.
  • Prior work. Checked on 28 October and again on 14 November 2026: Scovell’s list (Oman, vol. V, app. XV), Du Casse (Mémoires du roi Joseph, vol. IX), Marmont’s Mémoires (vol. IV), Jourdan, Wellington’s Dispatches and Supplementary Despatches, Daniel Bourdeau’s repository (target marmont1812, our reading), online search.
  • The illustration is a diagram of places, not an exact map. The image of the Spanish copy is in the record, with its credit.
